output.formulary_status: Timolol 0.5% eye drops and pyridostigmine: formulary.
interactions: Timolol eye drops (non-selective beta-blocker) in myasthenia gravis: a substantial part of each drop is absorbed systemically through the nasolacrimal mucosa; beta-blockers, oral and ophthalmic, have been reported to worsen neuromuscular transmission. Use with caution; consider an alternative.
Timolol with pyridostigmine: additive bradycardia; monitor heart rate when pyridostigmine is started.
Pyridostigmine with amlodipine, metformin or aspirin: no clinically relevant interaction.
warnings: Corticosteroids raise blood glucose; intensify glucose monitoring and diabetes treatment if prednisone is started.
Myasthenia gravis: avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium where possible; neuromuscular blockers need reduced doses with quantitative monitoring.

action_criteria.rationale: New fatigability, diurnal variation, bulbar and proximal weakness in a woman labelled CPEO: AChR antibodies are the first test and would overturn the label (Jacob 2025; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 16% in orbicularis oculi, 13% in nasalis and 11% in deltoid without facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: A decrement confirms a neuromuscular junction disorder; mitochondrial myopathy does not cause one (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MRD1 improves by 4 mm on each side after 3 minutes of ice, where it was negative at the first evaluation.

action_criteria.label: Order CT of the mediastinum with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with AChR-positive MG, and the result informs the thymectomy decision (Wolfe 2016). Renal function is normal for contrast with metformin.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 2.6 L (87% predicted, 32.9 mL/kg), MIP -58 cmH2O, MEP 74 cmH2O: normal.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Topical timolol is absorbed systemically, is a beta-blocker caution in MG and adds bradycardia with pyridostigmine; prostaglandin analogues are alternatives.
action_criteria.label: Check her timolol eye drops against myasthenia
action_criteria.rationale: Ophthalmic beta-blockers are easily overlooked and can aggravate MG; switching the glaucoma treatment is a concrete management change.

action_criteria.label: Order single-fibre EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Not needed once RNS shows a decrement and AChR antibodies are positive.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic nuclear or mitochondrial variant in blood.
action_criteria.label: Order a mitochondrial gene panel
action_criteria.rationale: Only if doubt about coexisting CPEO remains after the MG work-up, for example a poor response to treatment of the fixed ophthalmoparesis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General guidance on MG diagnosis and management.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on MG diagnosis and management
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or mitochondrial (CPEO) cause before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
required_recommendations: Revise the diagnosis to AChR-positive generalized MG and explain it to the patient and her ophthalmologist; long-standing ophthalmoparesis may respond only partly to treatment.
Ask ophthalmology to replace timolol eye drops with a prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) or a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily and titrate to effect (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily).

If symptoms persist, add prednisone at a low dose titrated upward, with closer glucose monitoring and adjustment of her diabetes treatment, and a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing) for long-term treatment.

Discuss elective thymectomy once she is stable (consensus guidance: an option in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65, no thymoma on CT); MGTX enrolled patients within 5 years of onset, so the expected benefit is less certain if her long-standing ptosis was myasthenic.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG does not inform ptosis or bulbar weakness.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); normal reflexes and gait give no reason to look for Miller Fisher syndrome.
FDG-PET has no place in the work-up of MG or CPEO.
No cardiac symptoms or murmur; the ECG shows no conduction defect.
Normal PR and QRS on the ECG and no syncope or palpitations; no conduction question to monitor.

accepted: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, presenting as long-standing 'ocular' disease previously misdiagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia

differential.key_features: Decades of progressive ptosis and fixed ophthalmoparesis fit CPEO, but new fatigability, diurnal variation, a now-positive ice pack test, an RNS decrement and AChR antibodies establish MG; normal lactate and CK. A coexisting mitochondrial myopathy is not excluded by blood genetics alone.
Ptosis with dysphagia and proximal weakness fits OPMD, but onset at 20, no family history, fatigability, decrement and AChR antibodies point to MG.
No ataxia, no conduction defect on the ECG, onset at 20 without systemic features.
Ophthalmic beta-blockers can aggravate MG but do not cause AChR antibodies or decades of ptosis.
Decades-long ocular presentation, preserved reflexes, no post-exercise facilitation, AChR antibodies positive.
No proptosis or lid retraction, no Graves history, normal TSH and free T4.

key_clinical_evidence: Ptosis since age 20 labelled CPEO, with eight months of new fatigability, diurnal variation, diplopia, bulbar fatigue, choking on liquids and fatigable hip flexor weakness.
Ice pack test now positive (4 mm each side) after a previously negative test.
AChR binding 5.8 nmol/L and a 3 Hz decrement in facial and deltoid muscles: AChR-positive generalized MG; the CPEO label is revised.
Timolol eye drops are a beta-blocker caution in MG and should be replaced.
No thymoma on CT; thymectomy is an option at 53 in AChR-positive generalized MG, with less certain benefit after a long ocular history; steroids will need closer glucose control in her diabetes.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: New fatigability, a now-positive ice pack test, an RNS decrement and AChR antibodies overturn the label.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior clinical diagnosis of CPEO with a negative ice pack test at the first evaluation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the CPEO label and pursue a mitochondrial work-up; miss MG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Extraocular muscle atrophy also occurs in long-standing MG; it does not distinguish the two.
red_herrings.data_point: Mild reduction of extraocular muscle volume on orbital MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the muscle atrophy as confirmation of a myopathic CPEO.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Topical timolol is absorbed systemically and is a beta-blocker caution in MG; replace it with a prostaglandin analogue.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Overlook a topical medicine as innocuous.

sequence_constraints.reason: Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

Creatinine, CK and lactate within reference range. AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In the MGTX trial thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

myasthenia gravis diagnosis and manageme.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by RNS or single-fibre EMG; chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In MGTX (Wolfe 2016) thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping of decades duration initially diagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — now worsening with new fatigability

family_history: Mother had hypertension and type 2 diabetes; no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease; no family history of similar ocular disease
past_medical_history: Elevated intraocular pressures (ocular hypertension), managed with timolol eye drops
Prior clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)

social_history.note: Teacher; married with three adult children; non-smoker; no alcohol; originally from Ghana, resident in UK for 18 years

patient.history_present_illness:
A 53-year-old Ghanaian woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral eyelid ptosis and increasing generalized fatigue. She first noticed left upper eyelid drooping at approximately age 20, which gradually worsened over years and was eventually followed by bilateral ptosis. She reported no diplopia, diurnal variation, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness throughout this time. She had multiple prior evaluations, and the consistent clinical picture (gradual onset without fatigability, no diplopia, absent ice pack test response at initial evaluation) led to a clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Over the past 8 months, however, she noticed new and different symptoms: significant fatigue with prolonged talking or chewing, muffled voice quality that was worse in the afternoon, and difficulty completing her usual 30-minute walk due to bilateral leg fatigue. She also experienced occasional choking with liquids. She noted for the first time that the eyelid drooping seemed more pronounced when tired and somewhat better in the morning, a pattern she had not observed before. She also reported a sensation of double images on lateral gaze, which resolved with eye closure.

Her ocular history included bilateral elevated intraocular pressures (managed with timolol eye drops) and bilateral cataract surgery 3 years prior (significant improvement in acuity post-operatively). She had no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease. On examination, complete bilateral ptosis was present. Restricted extraocular movements were present, more pronounced in vertical gaze. A new finding was fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation, absent in prior evaluations.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Restricted extraocular movements in all directions, more so in vertical gaze. Diplopia on extreme lateral gaze. Fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation (new finding). Pupils equal and reactive. No tongue fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Limb strength 5/5 in upper limbs. Hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable on sustained resistance). No fasciculations.

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild central adiposity; no organomegaly
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman; alert and cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible immediately; pseudophakic in both eyes, no proptosis or lid retraction. Weight 79 kg, height 160 cm.
physical_exam.neurological: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Extraocular movements restricted in all directions, more so in vertical gaze; no pain on eye movement. Diplopia elicitable on extreme lateral gaze but not in primary position. Fatigable palatal elevation on sustained phonation (new finding). No tongue fasciculations. Limb strength: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable), otherwise 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. Cerebellar examination normal. Sensation intact throughout. Gait normal.
